passage: Ulla had barely sat down at her grandmother's seventieth-birthday lunch in Tampere when Aunt Kirsi leaned over the herring. "Any special someone yet? You're twenty-one, you know." Two more relatives asked before the cake, each smiling, each warm. Ulla laughed the first time, said "Not yet" the second, and by the third she was studying the pattern on her napkin. Her cousin Abebe caught her eye and lifted the coffee pot as an excuse to stand. In the kitchen she pressed her palms on the cool counter. She knew Aunt Kirsi meant it kindly; Kirsi had married young and been happy. But every question made a wedding date feel closer, as if someone had wound a clock for her without asking.

qa.q: Where was the birthday lunch held?
qa.a: The lunch for Ulla's grandmother's seventieth birthday was in Tampere.

qa.q: How does Ulla feel by the third question, and what shows it?
qa.a: She feels pressed and uneasy. She studies her napkin, escapes to the kitchen and presses her palms on the counter, and she feels a clock has been wound for her. 🤍

qa.q: Which choice did Ulla make when the third question came, and how could she build on it?
qa.a: She stepped away to the kitchen to steady herself instead of snapping. Next she could thank Aunt Kirsi for caring, say she will share news when there is any, and turn the talk to something else, perhaps with Abebe's help.

qa.q: How might Aunt Kirsi see her own questions?
qa.a: As affection. Kirsi married young and was happy, so she probably means to wish Ulla the same joy without noticing how often the question comes.

grounding: A young adult hears relatives ask about marriage at a family gathering and feels the decision being hurried, though the concern is kind.

passage: Every tiffin hour at the design studio in Pune had turned into the same quiz. "Abhinav, twenty-two now, no? Time to look at a few biodatas," said Mr. Kulkarni from accounts, and two others nodded. Abhinav, who had joined only four months earlier, opened his mouth to say "Send me one, sir," just to end the subject. He stopped when he heard how tired the sentence sounded. Sangeeta, the senior editor, put down her spoon. "Sir, he'll tell us when there's news. Could you pass the pickle?" Later, at the water cooler, she said quietly, "They mean well. But you don't owe anyone an answer by Diwali." Abhinav nodded, surprised at how much lighter his shoulders felt.

qa.q: Who asked Abhinav about biodatas at the tiffin table?
qa.a: Mr. Kulkarni from accounts asked, and two others nodded.

qa.q: Why was Abhinav about to say "Send me one, sir"?
qa.a: He was tired of the topic and wanted the questions to stop. He felt hurried, not ready, and nearly agreed just for peace.

qa.q: Which choice kept Abhinav from a hurried yes, and what could he say himself next time?
qa.a: He stopped when he heard how tired his own sentence sounded, and Sangeeta backed him up. Next time he could politely say he will share news when there is any and change the subject.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta have been thinking when she spoke up?
qa.a: She probably saw that Abhinav was cornered and did not want him to agree just to end it, while still accepting that Mr. Kulkarni meant well.

grounding: A young adult is repeatedly asked about marriage at work and nearly agrees to a match only to stop the pressure.

passage: Sit down, Ishita, you keep asking how your Dadi and I said yes to each other. I am Shankar, and I was a young man of twenty-one with one good shirt. My father showed me a photograph and I agreed only to meet her. We sat in her uncle's front room in Nashik, both families on the sofas, the tea far too sweet. Her father asked about my wages. Your Dadi, Lata, asked what I thought of a wife who kept teaching. Her mother's face tightened, but Lata's eyes stayed on me. Afterwards I told my father, "I like her, but she decides freely, and I will wait even for a no." She asked for three days and one more meeting, on the verandah with the door open. I kept checking the gate all three days, hoping, and telling myself a no would be hers to give. On the fifth day she said yes.

qa.q: Where did the two families meet?
qa.a: They met in Lata's uncle's front room in Nashik, with both families on the sofas.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling during the three days of waiting, and what shows it?
qa.a: Shankar was hopeful but nervous. He kept checking the gate while telling himself a no would be Lata's to give.

qa.q: Which choice by young Shankar kept the match from being rushed?
qa.a: He told his father that Lata decides freely and that he would wait even for a no, which gave her three days and another meeting.

qa.q: How might Lata have felt when Shankar said he would accept a no?
qa.a: Probably relieved and more trusting, since she could answer honestly without fear of anger.

grounding: A young adult takes part in an arranged match, meets the other person with both families present, and both keep the freedom to refuse.

passage: The power cut came ten minutes into the meeting, and monsoon rain hammered the tin awning over the Nagpur flat. Kavitha, twenty-one, sat in the candlelit hall with her parents on one side and Vikram's parents on the other. The visitors' train left at nine. Vikram's sister Sarika lit a second candle and whispered, "Ask him everything, we haven't got long." Kavitha did: would he mind her keeping her teaching post, who cooked at his house, what he did when he was angry. Vikram answered without glancing at his parents. When the taxi honked outside, Kavitha said, "I'd like to meet once more, just the two of us over chai, before I say yes or no." "And if it's no, that's an honest answer," Vikram said. Both mothers, surprised, nodded.

qa.q: What happened ten minutes into the meeting?
qa.a: The power cut came, and monsoon rain hammered the tin awning over the Nagpur flat.

qa.q: What might Kavitha be feeling as she asks about her teaching post and his temper?
qa.a: She is determined and serious, wanting to know the real person before deciding. She is probably a little nervous too, but she spends the short time on questions rather than politeness.

qa.q: What choice did Kavitha make when the taxi honked, and why did it help?
qa.a: She asked for a second meeting, just the two of them, before answering. It gave time and a chance to talk freely, and let both say plainly whether they want to go on.

qa.q: How does Vikram seem to see Kavitha's request for another meeting?
qa.a: He accepts it calmly and treats a no as an honest answer, so he sees the match as a decision for both of them.

grounding: A young adult meets a prospective partner with both families present and asks for more time, keeping the right to say no.

passage: Dear Samir, You asked how the meeting with Meenal's biodata went. On paper: good height, good job, the same community, and my mother glowing. I almost stopped reading at that point. But I met her four times in six weeks: two walks, one lunch with her sister, and one long evening when the bus broke down. She talks about her students the way some people talk about cricket. When I spilled my chai, she laughed, then wiped the neighbouring table too. She disagrees with me about money and says so plainly, and I trust that more than any number on the sheet. Neither of us mentioned height or caste even once. I would like to tell both families that we want to keep meeting. Write back and tell me if I'm being silly. Lokesh

qa.q: How many times did Lokesh meet Meenal over six weeks?
qa.a: Lokesh met her four times: two walks, a lunch with her sister and one long evening when the bus broke down.

qa.q: What does "tell me if I'm being silly" suggest Lokesh feels?
qa.a: Lokesh feels admiration and trust for Meenal but is a little unsure, wanting Samir's view before telling the families. 🙂

qa.q: Which choice by Lokesh gave a fuller picture than the biodata?
qa.a: Lokesh met Meenal several times in different settings and noticed how she treats people and how plainly she disagrees about money.

qa.q: How might Meenal have experienced those six weeks of meetings?
qa.a: Probably as time to be known as a person: she talked about her students, disagreed openly about money, and was not judged only by a list.

grounding: A young adult looks past the biodata's height, job and community to how the other person behaves over repeated meetings.

passage: Okay, so when Mummy handed me the biodata for Jatin, it said what they all say: height, salary, caste, hobbies, "fond of cooking". I told her I would talk to him before deciding anything. We spoke on three weekends, first on video, then on a walk by the lake. I asked how he handles a bad day. He said he goes quiet and then apologises; I said I go loud and then apologise; we both laughed. He asked follow-up questions and actually waited for the answers. He told me his sister disagrees with him on nearly everything and he likes it. None of that was on the sheet. I haven't said yes yet. But I'm deciding about a person, not a page. Disha

qa.q: How many weekends did Disha and Jatin talk?
qa.a: They spoke on three weekends, first on video and then on a walk by the lake.

qa.q: What is Disha feeling about Jatin, and what shows it?
qa.a: Disha feels hopeful and interested. They laughed together and Jatin listened, but Disha stays cautious because nothing is decided yet.

qa.q: What choice did Disha make on receiving the biodata, and what did it give?
qa.a: Disha asked to talk with Jatin before deciding anything. Over three weekends that showed things the sheet never did, such as how he handles a bad day and how he listens.

qa.q: What might Jatin have felt when Disha asked how he handles a bad day?
qa.a: Probably surprised and pleased to be asked about something real. His honest answer and the shared laugh suggest he felt at ease.

grounding: A young adult sets aside the biodata's list and learns about the other person through several long conversations.

passage: Sunday, 11 pm. Three years of hiding Disha, and tonight I told someone. Molly Aunty came for tea and I said it out loud: there is someone, she is from another community, and I am terrified of what Appa will say. At six I had a text half typed to Appa, "Meet her or I leave." I deleted it. Molly Aunty said ultimatums shut doors that patience might open. She went quiet for a long minute, then asked what Disha is like. I talked for twenty minutes. Not a yes, but nobody shouted. She said to give Amma time, and she will come with me to speak to Appa after Christmas. My hands are still shaking, but my chest feels less tight. Scared. A little lighter too. Jomon

qa.q: Who came for tea and heard about Disha?
qa.a: Molly Aunty came for tea, and Jomon told her about Disha.

qa.q: Why did Jomon delete the half-typed text to Appa, and how does Jomon feel by the end?
qa.a: After Molly Aunty said ultimatums shut doors that patience might open, Jomon deleted it. By the end Jomon feels scared but a little lighter, with shaking hands and a less tight chest.

qa.q: Which choice by Jomon opened some ground, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Jomon deleted the ultimatum text and told Molly Aunty honestly. That led to a listening conversation and an offer to help speak with Appa after Christmas.

qa.q: How might Molly Aunty have felt when she heard about Disha?
qa.a: Probably surprised at first. She went quiet for a long minute and then asked what Disha is like, which shows curiosity and care rather than anger.

grounding: A young adult in love with someone from another community, afraid of family anger, confides in a trusted elder instead of issuing an ultimatum.

passage: Thursday night, chat. Pradeep: Ayesha wants to meet my parents. I said "next month" again. Third time now 😔 Tushar: What are you scared of? Pradeep: I've kept her secret from them for a year. Papa keeps saying "my son will marry within the community." She's from Hyderabad and she's Muslim. He'll shout. Tushar: What about Dada? He listens to you. Pradeep: True. He taught me chess and never once lectured me. Tushar: Then tell him first. Not "I'm marrying her", just who she is. Pradeep: No ultimatum for Papa? Tushar: Ultimatums make people dig in. Give them time. Pradeep: Okay. I'll take Dada for a walk on Sunday. Wish me luck 🙏 Tushar: Luck. Text me after.

qa.q: Which game did Dada teach Pradeep?
qa.a: Dada taught Pradeep chess and never lectured him.

qa.q: Why does Pradeep keep saying "next month"?
qa.a: Pradeep is afraid Papa will shout because Ayesha is from another community, so he keeps putting off the meeting.

qa.q: What choice does Pradeep make by the end of the chat, and why is it wiser than an ultimatum?
qa.a: He decides to take Dada for a walk on Sunday and talk first, because ultimatums make people dig in and time gives room.

qa.q: What would change for Papa if Pradeep opened with an ultimatum?
qa.a: Papa would likely dig in and get angrier, as Tushar warns. Hearing about Ayesha later, after a calm talk with Dada, gives Papa time.

grounding: A young adult hiding a relationship across communities fears family anger and, with a friend's advice, chooses a patient talk with a trusted elder.

passage: Late evening, text messages. Usha: Bhaiya, Amma just said everything is settled. Engagement in two weeks. They only need my nod. Shankar: Do you want it? Usha: I have met him for twenty minutes. I don't even know where we would live. Shankar: Then you're allowed to ask for more time. And for answers. Usha: What if Amma is hurt? She has already told the aunts. Shankar: Then she's hurt for a week. You saying yes out of fear is worse for both of you. Usha: And if my answer is no? Shankar: Then it's no. I'll tell Papa and Amma myself that nobody gets punished for it. Usha: Will you come when I ask for two more meetings? Shankar: I'll be sitting right next to you.

qa.q: How long has Usha met the man?
qa.a: Usha has met him for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What is Usha worried about when she says Amma has already told the aunts?
qa.a: Usha worries that Amma will be hurt and that refusing will bring anger, so Usha feels pressed to say yes.

qa.q: Which turning point in the chat makes it safe for Usha to ask for time?
qa.a: Shankar says a no is allowed and nobody will be punished for it, and he promises to sit next to Usha when Usha asks for two more meetings.

qa.q: How might Amma feel if Usha asks for time?
qa.a: Amma may feel hurt or embarrassed because she has told the aunts. As Shankar says, that hurt would pass, and hearing the request kindly with him there may help.

grounding: A young adult is told everything is settled and only a nod is needed; time, information and a safe route to refuse are then offered.

passage: After the paddy was stacked, Bhupen's father called the family into the courtyard of their village home near Jorhat. "Everything is fixed with Vandana's people," he said, beaming. "The date is in Magh. Only your nod is needed." Bhupen's mother passed round the betel-nut without looking up. Bhupen, twenty-five, had spoken to Vandana once, at a cousin's wedding, for a few minutes. His throat felt dry. "Baba, I'd like a fortnight. I want to meet her and her father, with my sister there, before I say anything." His father's smile went stiff. "Asking is not an insult," Bhupen's mother said quietly. Days later, on her veranda, Vandana told him she too had been told only a nod was needed. "I'm glad you asked," she said. "Ask me anything, and know that I can say no too."

qa.q: Where did Bhupen's father make the announcement?
qa.a: In the courtyard of their village home near Jorhat, after the paddy was stacked.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when his father said only a nod was needed?
qa.a: Bhupen felt nervous and pressed, with a dry throat, since he had spoken to Vandana only briefly. Still, he wanted time.

qa.q: What did Bhupen ask for that made real consent possible?
qa.a: He asked for a fortnight and a meeting with Vandana and her father, with his sister present, so he could get to know her and answer freely.

qa.q: How does Vandana see Bhupen's request?
qa.a: She is glad he asked. She had been told only a nod was needed too, so his request gives her the same chance to ask questions and to say no.

grounding: A young man is told everything is settled and only his nod is needed, and asks for time and information before answering.

passage: Kashish sat on the charpai in Leela's courtyard in a small Rajasthan town, sipping tea while Leela's father spread three photographs on the cot. "This boy has a house and a steady shop. No bad habits, good family," he said, tapping each one. "When Chotu's daughter's match broke, the whole street talked for a year. I won't have that for Leela." His hands shook slightly as he straightened the pictures. Leela's mother kept refilling glasses. Leela herself looked at the gate and said only, "Papa, my diploma ends in March." Her father nodded and went on about the shop. Kashish, Leela's friend since school, felt her chest tighten. She could see how much he loved his daughter, and how little of the plan had asked her.

qa.q: How many photographs did Leela's father spread on the cot?
qa.a: He spread three photographs on the cot.

qa.q: What is Kashish feeling as she watches Leela's father?
qa.a: Kashish feels torn and worried. She sees his love for his daughter, but her chest tightens because Leela has not been asked what she wants.

qa.q: What could Kashish choose to do after the visit to help both Leela and Leela's father?
qa.a: Kashish could encourage Leela to tell her father calmly what she wants, such as finishing her diploma, and gently suggest that Leela's own view belongs in a safe, respectable match.

qa.q: Why might Leela's father hurry with the photographs?
qa.a: He fears the street talking for a year if a match breaks, as it did for Chotu's daughter. He hurries out of care and worry, even though he is not yet listening to Leela.

grounding: A friend sees a girl's parents searching for a safe, respectable match out of care and fear of gossip, without yet asking her what she wants.

passage: Lunch break at the bakery in Rosario, and Pablo's phone buzzed for the third time. Ivan, cutting rolls beside him, heard Pablo's half of it: "Mamá, I know she's a doctor's daughter... yes, from a good family... no, I'm not saying no, I'm saying slowly." After hanging up, Pablo rubbed his forehead. "She has a list. Safe job, respected surname, someone the church ladies will approve of. A neighbour's daughter's marriage fell apart last year and half the barrio whispered." Ivan noticed that Pablo never said a bad word about his mother. Ivan also noticed that Pablo hadn't said what he himself hoped for. "What do you want?" Ivan asked. Pablo laughed, surprised. "Nobody's asked me that yet."

qa.q: Where is the bakery?
qa.a: The bakery is in Rosario.

qa.q: What does Ivan notice about Pablo that shows how Pablo feels toward his mother?
qa.a: Pablo never says a bad word about her, which suggests he loves her and understands her fear, though he is stuck between her plan and his own unspoken hopes.

qa.q: What turning point came when Ivan asked "What do you want?"
qa.a: It gave Pablo a chance to say what he himself wants, which nobody had asked, and could lead to a fuller talk with his mother.

qa.q: How might Pablo's mother see the search for a match?
qa.a: As care. She wants someone safe and respected, and fears the barrio whispering, as it did when a neighbour's daughter's marriage fell apart.

grounding: A bystander overhears one side of a parent's call about a safe, respectable match, sees care behind it, and notices the young person's own wishes are unspoken.

passage: Dear Tenzin, Thank you for meeting me twice and for being so patient while I took ten days to answer. My answer is no, and I want to give you the reasons rather than leave you guessing. I would like to finish my research posting in Pune, and you hope to move to Dharamshala soon; I do not want either of us to give up a plan we love. I said the same to my parents this week, calmly, and I will say it again if they ask again. I enjoyed our conversations and would be glad to stay in touch as friends, if you'd like that. I also know an old classmate who is hoping to meet someone, and I will introduce you only if you want me to. Warm wishes, Vinita

qa.q: How many days did Vinita take to answer?
qa.a: Vinita took ten days to answer.

qa.q: What is Vinita feeling while writing, and what shows it?
qa.a: Vinita feels calm, kind and firm. Vinita gives reasons, thanks Tenzin and repeats the no without harshness.

qa.q: Which choices in Vinita's letter made the refusal easier for Tenzin to hear?
qa.a: Vinita gave clear reasons, thanked Tenzin for the patience, offered friendship and an optional introduction, and blamed no one.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Probably disappointed but respected, since Vinita took time, gave honest reasons and stayed warm.

grounding: A young adult declines a match with reasons, alternatives and a considered delay, and repeats the calm no to their own parents.

passage: So Jyoti Masi rang again about the match, the third time this month. I had already taken a week to think. This time I said, "Masi, thank you for caring enough to search. My answer is no. I want to finish my nursing course, and I don't feel anything for him." She said, "Just meet him once." I said, "I understand you want me settled. The answer is still no, but I'd love to visit you on Sunday." She tried again about the family being so good. I repeated it kindly, same words, no shouting. My hands were cold the whole call. At the end she sighed and said, "You sound like your mother." I couldn't tell if it was a compliment. But on Sunday she made my favourite kheer, and nobody mentioned the boy. Charu

qa.q: What did Charu want to finish?
qa.a: Charu wanted to finish the nursing course.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling during the call, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Charu felt nervous but stayed calm. Charu's hands were cold the whole call, yet the same kind answer was repeated without shouting.

qa.q: Which choice did Charu make on the call, and what did it achieve that a sudden fight might not?
qa.a: Charu repeated the same kind no. The kind, repeated no kept the bond with Jyoti Masi warm, as the Sunday visit and kheer show, while the answer never changed.

qa.q: How might Jyoti Masi have felt when Charu said no again?
qa.a: Probably disappointed and worried, since she sighed, but still caring, as the Sunday kheer shows.

grounding: A young adult who does not want a match says so with reasons, takes time, offers a visit instead, and repeats the calm no kindly.

passage: Tuesday. At the family dinner in Bhopal, Uncle asked, "Mahima, twenty-five now, when do we eat your wedding sweets?" Mahima put down her fork. "Not yet, Uncle. I'm building my architecture practice." His eyebrows rose; she went red and changed the subject. Friday. Her cousin Asif rang. "Mama is telling everyone you're too fussy." Mahima breathed out. "I'm not fussy. I'm busy, and I'm happy. If that changes, you'll hear it from me first." The next Sunday, when Uncle started again, Mahima smiled. "I know you care. My answer is the same: not yet. Come and see my first site instead." Uncle blinked, then laughed. "Fine. But I'm bringing sweets to the site."

qa.q: On which day did Asif ring Mahima?
qa.a: Asif rang on Friday.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling at the first dinner, and how did it show?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and flustered. She put down her fork, went red and changed the subject.

qa.q: What changed between Tuesday and the following Sunday in how Mahima answered?
qa.a: On Tuesday she went red and changed the subject. By Sunday she smiled, kindly said "not yet" again and invited Uncle to see her first site.

qa.q: How does Uncle seem to take Mahima's steady answer on Sunday?
qa.a: He blinks, then laughs and agrees, promising sweets at the site, so he seems to accept it and feel included. 🙂

grounding: A young adult who wants to build a career faces questions about marriage and, over several days, holds a clear, steady boundary.

passage: You ask why I never felt sorry for being single at twenty-five, Nilesh? Sit, I will tell you. I am Kavitha, and back then I was a young nurse in Mysuru, just through a hard year when I lost my mother. Every relative asked, "What age now? When will we hear the shehnai?" My father called me to the verandah and said the proposals were piling up. I was trembling, but I said, "Appa, I need two years, for work and for myself. I will tell you when I am ready, and I will tell you if I never am." He was silent a long time. Then he said, "Then I will tell them you have work to do." My aunt clicked her tongue for months. I did not mind. I chose my time, and it was mine.

qa.q: Where was young Kavitha working as a nurse?
qa.a: Kavitha was working as a young nurse in Mysuru.

qa.q: How did young Kavitha feel as she spoke to Appa on the verandah?
qa.a: Kavitha was trembling and nervous, yet steady about what was wanted: two years for Kavitha's own work and needs.

qa.q: What choice did young Kavitha make on the verandah that shaped what followed?
qa.a: Kavitha told Appa calmly that two years were needed and that Kavitha would say when ready, instead of just agreeing or arguing.

qa.q: How did Kavitha's father seem to feel about the request?
qa.a: After a long silence he agreed and offered to tell the relatives that Kavitha had work to do, which suggests he was thoughtful and willing to support the choice.

grounding: A young adult chooses to wait to marry, states the boundary clearly to family, and shows that the delay was a choice.

subtype: Girls taught to save for marriage [Receiver]
passage: Dear Bua, Last Sunday Papa was doing the accounts and said, "Vijay's coaching fees come first. Rekha, start saving for your shaadi." He said it lightly, and Dadi nodded: "A daughter's share is her wedding." I smiled and washed the dishes, but all night I felt like a bill someone had to pay. I am fifteen and I came first in maths, Bua. Then yesterday Mummy mentioned your call, and Papa put his tea down. He said, "Both of you will study as far as you wish. Wedding savings can wait." I didn't know what to say. My brother Vijay looked up and said, "Then we both get the tutor." I am still learning to believe it. Please come for Diwali. Rekha

qa.q: What did Papa say came first?
qa.a: Papa said Vijay's coaching fees come first.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel after Papa's remark, and what shows it?
qa.a: Rekha felt like a burden, "a bill someone had to pay". She smiled and washed the dishes, but the feeling stayed all night.

qa.q: What turning point in the letter changed things for Rekha?
qa.a: After Mummy mentioned Bua's call, Papa put his tea down and said both children will study as far as they wish and wedding savings can wait.

qa.q: How does Vijay seem to see the new arrangement?
qa.a: He accepts it as fair and offers to share the tutor with Rekha, which shows he stands with her.

grounding: A teenage girl is told to save for her wedding while her brother's coaching comes first, and equal schooling is then offered.

subtype: Girls taught to save for marriage [Receiver]
passage: Kirti, listen, I have to tell someone. At Shweta didi's wedding yesterday, Fufa was eating jalebi and told Mummy loudly, "Put money aside for Lalita's shaadi. Spend on the boy's coaching. Vijay's the one who'll earn." Mummy was holding a plate. I stood right beside her. I'm fourteen, the girl in the family whose marks were higher than my brother's last term, but suddenly I felt like a cost that needed managing. My ears went hot. I wanted to vanish behind the stage flowers. Then Mummy said, quite calmly, "Both my children will study as far as they want, Bhaiya. Lalita's fees are fees, not a wedding fund." Fufa shrugged and reached for another jalebi. Vijay whispered, "I'll buy you a pen for your exam." It was such a small thing. But I'm still smiling.

qa.q: Who said to put money aside for Lalita's shaadi?
qa.a: Fufa said it, at Shweta didi's wedding.

qa.q: What was Lalita feeling when Fufa spoke?
qa.a: Lalita felt hurt and embarrassed, like a cost that needed managing. Lalita's ears went hot and the wish was to vanish behind the stage flowers.

qa.q: What turning point came when Mummy spoke, and how did it help Lalita?
qa.a: Mummy calmly said both children will study and fees are fees, not a wedding fund, so Lalita was defended without a fight.

qa.q: How does Vijay seem to feel about his sister's situation?
qa.a: Vijay appears to stand with Lalita. He whispers that he will buy a pen for the exam, a small sign of support.

grounding: A teenage girl hears that her brother's education comes first and a wedding fund is hers, then her mother insists on equal schooling.

passage: At nine the night before the engagement, Yogesh found the typed list on the dining table: fridge, gold set, cash for the caterer, "as per custom." His father wanted it couriered to Aditi's family by morning. Yogesh, twenty-two, picked it up. His father was already reaching for the phone. "Papa, wait," he said. "I won't take any of this, and our wedding does not hinge on it." His father frowned. "Many families do it, beta. Otherwise people will say..." "Then let them say it about me," Yogesh replied evenly. "Please don't send it. I'll call Aditi's father myself tonight and tell him so." His grandmother, listening from the doorway, said quietly, "Let the boy speak." The list went into the bin, and Yogesh made the call with steady hands.

qa.q: What items were on the typed list?
qa.a: The list had a fridge, a gold set and cash for the caterer.

qa.q: What is Yogesh feeling when he says "Then let them say it about me"?
qa.a: Yogesh feels determined and calm but respectful. He stands firm despite his father's frown, and his hands stay steady.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do that protected Aditi's family?

passage: On Saturday morning in their Ahmedabad flat, Ojas waited until his mother Hansa had poured the tea. "Mummy, before we meet Neha's parents next week, I need to say something. I won't accept dowry in any form. Not cash, not a car, not a grand hall they have to borrow for. The wedding won't depend on it." Hansa's cup stopped halfway. "Beta, what will Bhabhi and the others say? People like to ask what the girl's side is giving." Ojas kept his voice level. "I know you worry about the relatives. But I'd be ashamed to begin a marriage on a price. Can you help me tell them, or at least not push?" Hansa was silent, then sighed. "Your father wanted the same at your age and never said it. Maybe you'll manage it." She reached across and squeezed his hand.

qa.q: When did Ojas speak to his mother?
qa.a: On Saturday morning, before meeting Neha's parents the next week.

qa.q: What is Ojas feeling as he says he would be ashamed to begin a marriage on a price?
qa.a: Ojas feels resolved and a little anxious. He keeps his voice level but is deeply firm about wanting his integrity.

qa.q: What did Ojas do that made the talk easier for his mother?
qa.a: He spoke early, firmly and respectfully, admitted he knew she worried about the relatives, and asked for her help.

qa.q: How does Hansa move from worry to something like acceptance?
qa.a: She first worries about what relatives will say. Then she sighs, says perhaps he will manage it, and squeezes his hand, showing love and some pride. ❤️

grounding: A young man tells his family early and respectfully that he will not take dowry and the wedding will not depend on it.
